title: 5.5 Cardiovascular and Respiratory Responses to Anaerobic Exercise

cards.front: What peak blood pressure and heart rate values can occur during high-intensity anaerobic exercise such as a heavy leg press?
cards.back: Peak blood pressure can reach extreme surges of up to 320/250 mmHg (particularly during the concentric sticking point), accompanied by heart rates approaching 170 beats/min.

cards.front: How does the Valsalva maneuver alter intrathoracic pressure and stroke volume kinetics during heavy lifting?
cards.back: Expiring against a closed glottis increases intrathoracic pressure, compressing the vena cava and temporarily reducing venous return and end-diastolic volume. As a result, stroke volume and cardiac output peak during the eccentric phase or immediate rest period, and heart rate peaks within 5 seconds post-set.

cards.front: What acute changes occur to plasma volume and muscular blood flow during and immediately after high-intensity resistance contractions?
cards.back: Muscular contractions exceeding 20% of maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) compress capillaries, creating transient vascular occlusion and acute plasma volume reductions of up to 22%. Muscular relaxation post-set triggers a surge in blood flow known as reactive hyperemia.

cards.front: What chronic reductions occur to resting heart rate and resting blood pressure following long-term anaerobic training?
cards.back: Long-term anaerobic training reduces resting heart rate by 4% to 13% (yielding resting values of 60 to 78 beats/min) and reduces resting systolic and diastolic blood pressure by 2% to 4%, primarily by decreasing peripheral vascular resistance.

cards.front: What is the Rate-Pressure Product (RPP), and how does chronic resistance training affect this clinical metric at rest?
cards.back: Rate-Pressure Product is calculated as RPP = HR x SBP and measures myocardial oxygen consumption. Chronic resistance training maintains or significantly decreases resting RPP, reflecting enhanced myocardial efficiency and lower resting cardiac workload.

cards.front: What structural changes occur to the left ventricular walls in chronically resistance-trained athletes?
cards.back: Heavy resistance training induces concentric cardiac remodeling, characterized by an increased absolute posterior left ventricular wall thickness and interventricular septum wall thickness. When expressed relative to lean body mass, wall thickness remains within normal physiological limits.

cards.front: How do chronic adaptations in left ventricular chamber volume differ between heavy powerlifters and bodybuilders?
cards.back: Heavy low-volume powerlifting produces little to no change in left ventricular chamber volume. In contrast, bodybuilders exhibit expanded left ventricular and atrial chamber volumes due to high-volume, short-rest training protocols and aerobic conditioning.

cards.front: How does chronic resistance training modify the acute hemodynamic response to a given absolute submaximal workload?
cards.back: Chronic training blunts acute surges in heart rate, blood pressure, and rate-pressure product during submaximal lifting, reducing sympathetic drive and protecting the myocardium during exercise.

cards.front: What is afterload, and how does its chronic reduction improve cardiac output during resistance exercise?
cards.back: Afterload is the peripheral arterial resistance against which the left ventricle must pump blood. Chronic training reduces arterial resistance and afterload, allowing the heart to achieve a significantly higher peak stroke volume and peak cardiac output (Q) during exertion.

cards.front: When does peak pulmonary ventilation (VE) occur relative to a set of heavy resistance exercise, and what factors maximize it?
cards.back: Pulmonary ventilation reaches its peak (exceeding 60 L/min) during the first minute of recovery following set completion (recovery overshoot). Short rest intervals (30 to 60 seconds) produce the highest peak ventilatory rates due to metabolic H+ and CO2 accumulation.

cards.front: How does chronic anaerobic training adapt breathing frequency (f) and tidal volume (VT) during submaximal versus maximal exercise?
cards.back:
• Submaximal Exercise: Decreases breathing frequency while increasing tidal volume (deeper, slower respiration), optimizing alveolar ventilation.
  • Maximal Exercise: Increases both tidal volume and breathing frequency to maximize peak gas exchange.

cards.front: What change occurs to the ventilatory equivalent for oxygen (VE/VO2) following chronic anaerobic training, and what does this signify?
cards.back: Chronic training lowers the VE/VO2 ratio during exercise, signifying improved ventilatory efficiency where less minute ventilation is required per unit of oxygen consumed by active skeletal muscle.
